reasons: No tests are visible in this file.
Many overlapping keyword patterns can misfire, and the code's own comments mention deliberate exclusions to avoid this.
The placement functions are outside the sections given, so their behaviour cannot be checked from this file alone.

terms.meaning: A pattern of text that a program uses to recognise words, such as all names containing tower or mast.
The numbered list of work items a project uses to break its scope into parts.
Primavera P6, a common scheduling software program that stores project activities and dates.
A group of related industries or kinds that share one layout style, such as solar or marine.
Distance measured along a line, such as kilometres along a road or pipeline.
A Python way to define a simple record that just holds named values.
A number giving an element its order in a flow, such as from pit to plant to tailings.

sections.name: File setup (part 1)
sections.title: Module purpose and industry descriptions
sections.what: Explains what the file does and holds a short plain-text description for each industry's layout style, such as the solar grid or the mine flow. These descriptions are meant to be shown with the layout to say it is schematic.
sections.why: Likely reason: the owner needs a reminder that positions are assumptions, so each style carries a note saying so.
sections.watch_out: The description text is shown with each layout, so changing a family name here must match the family names used elsewhere.

sections.name: File setup (part 2)
sections.title: Keyword lists for each industry family
sections.what: Lists the words that suggest each industry family, such as solar, wind, mining, building or marine. These lists decide which industry layout a project receives.
sections.why: Likely reason: the building list uses only strong words, because equipment words like pump or tank also appear in ordinary building services.
sections.watch_out: The hydro list deliberately has no bare dam word, since a tailings dam belongs to the mine, so adding one would misfile mining projects.

sections.name: Kind
sections.title: Shape of an element kind
sections.what: Defines the record that describes one kind of element: its name, family, recognition pattern, 3D shape, default size and stage number. The stage defaults to zero.
sections.why: Likely reason: each kind is described the same way so one matching routine can handle all of them.
sections.watch_out: Stage numbers only mean flow order in mining and process layouts, so setting one elsewhere has no visible effect.

sections.name: _k (part 1)
sections.title: Wind, solar and storage element kinds
sections.what: Lists the kinds for wind turbines, met masts, solar blocks, inverters, solar fields, battery storage, power conversion units and telecom towers, in order from most specific to least specific.
sections.why: Likely reason: the most specific patterns come first so a turbine is not mistaken for a generic block.
sections.watch_out: Inverter words appear under both solar and storage, so the earlier solar entry wins for those names.

sections.name: _k (part 2)
sections.title: Airport, port and tunnel station kinds
sections.what: Lists the kinds for control towers, hangars, terminals, runways, taxiways, aprons, quay cranes, offshore platforms, breakwaters, container yards, dredging and berths, plus tunnel portals and stations. The station pattern excludes pump and lift stations.
sections.why: Likely reason: the exclusions stop pumping stations from being drawn as tunnel stations.
sections.watch_out: The container yard pattern matches any word yard, so an unrelated yard can be drawn as a container stack.

sections.name: _k (part 3)
sections.title: Tunnel, dam and hydro element kinds
sections.what: Lists the kinds for tunnel boring machines, shafts, cross passages, drives, spillways, intakes, penstocks, powerhouses, surge tanks, cofferdams, tailraces, reservoirs and dam blocks and bodies. Specific hydro parts come before the generic dam entry.
sections.why: Likely reason: specific parts are checked first so a penstock is not drawn as a whole dam.
sections.watch_out: The dam block pattern matches any block with a number, so a non-dam block can be misread if its family is not filtered out first.

sections.name: _k (part 4)
sections.title: Process, power and water treatment kinds
sections.what: Lists the kinds for reactor buildings, LNG tanks, electrolysers, turbine halls, heat recovery boilers, transformers, cooling towers, flares, process columns, flotation tanks, headworks, digesters, clarifiers, disinfection basins and water towers. Each has a stage number for flow order.
sections.why: Likely reason: flow stages let process and treatment plants be drawn in the order materials move through them.
sections.watch_out: Words such as reactor and boiler appear in more than one entry, so list order decides which kind wins, and the transformer entry applies to any family.

sections.name: _k (part 5)
sections.title: Name rules for water, process and mining equipment
sections.what: This block is part of a long list of name rules. Each rule says which words in a schedule name mean a tank, pump station, basin, crusher, conveyor, mill, thickener, tailings area or open pit, and how large the drawn block should be. Together these rules decide the shape the app draws for each schedule item.
sections.why: Likely reason: a plain rule list lets the app recognise equipment from free-text names without a separate database.
sections.watch_out: Rules are tried from top to bottom and the first match wins, so moving or adding a rule above an existing one can change what many items become.

sections.name: _k (part 6)
sections.title: Name rules for linear, process and building items
sections.what: Continues the same rule list with rules for bridges, culverts, road segments, pumps and heaters, process units, stadiums, data halls, warehouses and general buildings. These rules set the shape and size of each drawn item.
sections.why: Likely reason: the rules are grouped by industry, so each industry's words stay together.
sections.watch_out: The word filter appears in both the basin rule and the pump rule, and the basin rule comes first, so filter items may be drawn as basins.

sections.name: _k (part 7)
sections.title: Catch-all building rule and sub-part role rules
sections.what: Ends the rule list with a broad building rule and picks the tower rule used for single-building projects. It also sets three word rules that label sub-items as foundation, civil or cable work, and anything else is labelled main.
sections.why: Likely reason: the sub-item labels let the app place footings, roads and cables around each main item.
sections.watch_out: The role rules are checked in order, so foundation words win over civil words when both appear in the same name.

sections.name: _k (part 8)
sections.title: Linear work layers and number and tag patterns
sections.what: Holds the build-order layers for roads, rail tracks and pipelines. Each layer has a word pattern, a drawn shape, a height, a height offset and a width. It also defines a pattern for equipment tags and a pattern for numbers inside names.
sections.why: Likely reason: the layer order follows how the work is built, with clearing first and surfacing last.
sections.watch_out: The tag pattern is defined here but is not used in the code shown, so do not assume it affects the output.

sections.name: Element
sections.title: The Element record for one recognised item
sections.what: Describes one recognised item: its path anchor, its kind, its industry family, and the schedule paths that belong to it, each with a role. It also gives the item a name, a sort key, and the first number found in its name.
sections.why: Likely reason: one record keeps all the schedule rows for one physical item together.
sections.watch_out: The number is taken from the first digits in the name, so a name with several numbers can pair with the wrong neighbour.

sections.name: _families
sections.title: Finding industry words in a path
sections.what: Returns every industry family whose keyword list appears in the given text, ignoring capital letters.
sections.why: Likely reason: lets the app tell which industry a schedule belongs to from its wording.
sections.watch_out: The keyword list is stored in FAMILY_WORDS, which is not shown here, so its contents must be checked separately.

sections.name: _kind_for
sections.title: Choosing the kind for one name part
sections.what: Walks the rule list and returns the first kind whose pattern matches a part of the path, as long as its family is allowed or it applies to any family.
sections.why: Likely reason: this is the single point where names become kinds, so every drawn item passes through it.
sections.watch_out: Because the first match wins, rule order decides the result, and an earlier broad rule can hide a later specific one.

sections.name: _deepest
sections.title: Finding the most specific named part
sections.what: Searches a schedule path from its deepest part upward and returns the first part that names a known kind. This is why a specific pump name is preferred over a general area name.
sections.why: Likely reason: the deepest name is usually the most specific description of the item.
sections.watch_out: When the shared flag is off, generic building matches are skipped, so changing that flag can hide an item that was previously found.

sections.name: _role
sections.title: Deciding the role of a sub-item
sections.what: Reads the text under a main item and returns foundation, civil, cable or the default main role.
sections.why: Likely reason: sub-items need a label so the layout can place them around the main item.
sections.watch_out: Unrecognised sub-items default to main, so a missing keyword can make a footing look like a second main piece of equipment.

sections.name: recognise
sections.title: Grouping schedule paths into items
sections.what: Turns a list of schedule paths into recognised items and a list of paths that could not be placed. Lines and substations are set aside for their own layout, and a single-building project treats its first part as the tower.
sections.why: Likely reason: many schedule rows can describe one physical item, so they are grouped under one anchor.
sections.watch_out: Paths left unplaced here are drawn later by a fallback layout, so an unknown name may appear in a different place from the industry zone.

sections.name: _Zone
sections.title: Holder for one industry's placed items
sections.what: Stores each item's position and shape by its schedule path, and works out the rectangle that covers all of them.
sections.why: Likely reason: a shared holder lets every industry layout be measured and shifted the same way.
sections.watch_out: Placing the same path twice silently replaces the earlier position.

sections.name: _extent
sections.title: Ground footprint of a rotated item
sections.what: Returns how much ground an item takes along the east-west and north-south directions after its rotation is applied.
sections.why: Likely reason: the footprint is needed so neighbouring items do not overlap when they are turned.
sections.watch_out: The calculation treats the item as a flat rectangle, so unusual shapes can be measured wrongly.

sections.name: _place_roles
sections.title: Placing one item with its supporting work
sections.what: Places an item's main shape at a point, then puts its foundation, civil pad and cable trench around it. Several items with the same role get small offsets so they do not sit on top of each other.
sections.why: Likely reason: keeps supporting work near the item it belongs to.
sections.watch_out: The offsets are fixed amounts, so closely packed items can overlap their neighbours' supporting work.

sections.name: _grid
sections.title: Choosing a near-square grid size
sections.what: Returns the number of columns for a grid that holds the given count of items, close to a square with a stretch factor.
sections.why: Likely reason: a near-square grid stops the drawing from becoming a long thin strip.
sections.watch_out: The result is always at least one column, so an empty group still reserves one column.

sections.name: _solar
sections.title: Solar field layout
sections.what: Lays solar blocks in a grid ordered by name, places each inverter station beside the block with the same number, and puts other items in a row to the south.
sections.why: Likely reason: inverter stations sit next to their solar block so the drawing shows which block each one serves.
sections.watch_out: Matching relies on numbers in names, so an inverter with no matching block is pushed into the southern row.

sections.name: _wind
sections.title: Wind farm layout
sections.what: Lines turbines up in strings of eight, alternates the offset of each string for spacing, and places all other items in a column on the western side.
sections.why: Likely reason: strings mirror how turbines are usually arranged along a cable run.
sections.watch_out: The last turbine in each string has its cable direction flipped, so changing the string size also changes where those cables point.

sections.name: _process
sections.title: Process plant layout
sections.what: Places process units in rows on two sides of a central spine, moves tank farms and utilities to the ends, and cuts pipe racks into equal lengths along the spine.
sections.why: Likely reason: tanks and utilities at the edges leave process units in a clear line.
sections.watch_out: Sides alternate by sorted name, so adding one unit can move every unit after it to the other side.

sections.name: _mining
sections.title: Mining site layout
sections.what: Places mining equipment in columns from left to right by stage number, runs conveyors in a band, and puts stage six items in a row at the south end.
sections.why: Likely reason: the columns follow the stage numbers set on each rule, so the drawing runs in process order.
sections.watch_out: Stages two and six are treated specially, so changing those numbers changes which items become conveyors or move to the south.

sections.name: _linear
sections.title: Linear route layout with numbered segments
sections.what: Chooses a road, rail or pipeline layer set from the words in the schedule. It then places each numbered segment in a line of fixed 40 metre spans, with bridges and culverts on the line and other structures beside it.
sections.why: Likely reason: each segment becomes a block in a row so the route reads as one continuous corridor.
sections.watch_out: The work type is guessed from loose keywords, so a rail word in any name can switch a road project to rail.

sections.name: _anchor_key
sections.title: Sort key for the full path
sections.what: Builds the key used to order items by their full path, so the drawing is laid out in a consistent order.
sections.why: Likely reason: a stable order keeps the layout the same from one run to the next.
sections.watch_out: The ordering depends on a helper named _natural, which is not shown here.

sections.name: _by_kind
sections.title: Grouping items by kind
sections.what: Collects items into groups keyed by kind name, with each group sorted by path.
sections.why: Likely reason: each layout takes out the kinds it handles by name.
sections.watch_out: Kinds that no layout picks up are left in the leftover group and placed in a generic row.

sections.name: _row
sections.title: Placing items side by side
sections.what: Puts a list of items in one row along the east-west direction with a set gap, and returns the position where the row ends.
sections.why: Likely reason: used for leftover items and for equipment that naturally lines up.
sections.watch_out: All items in a row share one north-south position, so their supporting work can collide with nearby rows.

sections.name: _below
sections.title: Text below the main item
sections.what: Returns the schedule path text that comes after the item's own name. This text is used to work out roles and floor levels.
sections.why: Likely reason: the item's name is already known, so only the extra detail is needed for matching.
sections.watch_out: If nothing follows the name, the result is empty, so callers must fall back to the item name.

sections.name: _layer
sections.title: First matching layer
sections.what: Returns the first layer whose word pattern matches a file name, or a default layer if none match.
sections.why: Likely reason: lets each kind of work pick its own drawn layer.
sections.watch_out: Layers are checked from top to bottom, so the order of entries in the layer list decides the result.

sections.name: _level
sections.title: Reading a floor number from a name
sections.what: Looks for a floor or level number in a name, including forms such as Level 3, L3, basement and ground floor. Returns the number, or nothing if none is found.
sections.why: Likely reason: the floor decides the height at which each piece of building work is drawn.
sections.watch_out: The short L pattern and the basement pattern can match unrelated codes, which would place work on the wrong floor.

sections.name: _building_work
sections.title: Classifying building work
sections.what: Labels a piece of building work as foundation, roof, facade, fit-out or general structure, using the first keyword that matches.
sections.why: Likely reason: each type of work gets its own drawn shape and height.
sections.watch_out: The first match wins, so a fit-out item whose name contains the word roof is drawn as roof work.

sections.name: _storeys
sections.title: Stacking a building by floor
sections.what: Draws each part of a building at its floor: foundations below ground, the roof at the top, facades as tall panels, fit-out as thin slabs and floors as plates. If no numbered floors above ground are found, the building is drawn as six storeys.
sections.why: Likely reason: lets a schedule with floor names become a stacked building drawing.
sections.watch_out: The six storey default applies silently to any building whose schedule has no floor numbers.

sections.name: _building
sections.title: Placing buildings in rows
sections.what: Places each building along the east-west direction and starts a new row after about 260 metres. Towers are stacked by floor, and other items are placed by their roles.
sections.why: Likely reason: keeps a site with many buildings within a readable width.
sections.watch_out: The 260 metre row limit is fixed in this function, so every site wraps at the same width whatever its shape.

sections.name: _strip
sections.title: Drawing one airfield strip
sections.what: Draws one runway, taxiway or apron strip along a set length, with clearing, earthwork, drainage, lighting and base layers laid in order.
sections.why: Likely reason: the layers mirror the build order of an airfield strip.
sections.watch_out: Work that matches no layer gets the strip's own paving, so an unrecognised item is drawn as a full paved surface.

sections.name: _airport
sections.title: Airport layout
sections.what: Stacks aprons, taxiways and runways on the airside, places terminals in a row near the main east-west line and hangars beside them, and puts the remaining items in a row on the far side of the airside.
sections.why: Likely reason: the terminal faces the airside so that boarding bridges can reach the aircraft stands.
sections.watch_out: The airside direction and the starting offset are fixed numbers, so changing either moves every strip and the terminal row together.

sections.name: _marine
sections.title: Port and marine layout
sections.what: Puts berths in a line along the quay, places quay cranes above the quay, arranges container yards in a grid, and sets dredging, breakwaters and offshore platforms out toward the sea.
sections.why: Likely reason: the sea-side items face the water, which matches how wharves are normally arranged.
sections.watch_out: The quay is at least 120 metres long even when the berths are shorter, so the drawing can run past the real berths.

sections.name: _hydro
sections.title: Dam and hydro power layout
sections.what: Lays out a dam across the valley along the east-west line. It places spillways, intakes, penstocks and the powerhouse on the downstream side, and puts reservoir and cofferdam items at fixed offsets.
sections.why: Likely reason: water flows from the reservoir through the intakes to the powerhouse, so the layout follows that path.
sections.watch_out: Many items use fixed offsets, so a project with many intakes or spillways may see its items overlap.

sections.name: _tunnel (part 1)
sections.title: Tunnel bores, machines and portals
sections.what: Lays each tunnel bore along the east-west line between its portals. Bores are grouped by direction name and each group is offset sideways, and tunnel boring machines are placed at the face of their drive.
sections.why: Likely reason: keeps the two directions of a twin tunnel visibly separate.
sections.watch_out: Bore names are matched with a pattern, so a drive whose name has no recognisable direction or bore word falls into the unnamed group.

sections.name: _tunnel (part 2)
sections.title: Stations, shafts and cross passages
sections.what: Spaces tunnel stations and shafts evenly along the tunnel, places cross passages between the bores, and lines up any remaining items in a row on the south side.
sections.why: Likely reason: even spacing is the simplest way to show access points along a tunnel.
sections.watch_out: The side offset is taken from the largest bore offset plus 30, so adding more bore groups moves the shaft row further away.

sections.name: _water
sections.title: Water treatment layout
sections.what: Places treatment stages from left to right in flow order, with each stage's items stacked from south to north. Stage six items are placed in a row at the front.
sections.why: Likely reason: a left-to-right order matches how water moves through a treatment plant.
sections.watch_out: The front row position is worked out from what was already placed, so changing the stage order moves the front row.

sections.name: _storage
sections.title: Battery storage layout
sections.what: Places batteries in a grid, puts each power conversion unit beside the battery with the same number, and places all other items in a row to the south.
sections.why: Likely reason: conversion units sit beside their battery row so each unit is easy to match to its battery.
sections.watch_out: Matching depends on numbers in names, and conversion units with no match are sent to the leftover row.

sections.name: _telecom
sections.title: Telecom tower layout
sections.what: Places telecom towers in a grid and puts other equipment in a row to the south.
sections.why: Likely reason: a grid keeps many towers compact and easy to read.
sections.watch_out: The grid size depends on the number of towers, so adding one tower can change the whole grid.

sections.name: corridor_layers
sections.title: Corridor layers for unnumbered routes
sections.what: For a linear project without numbered segments, stacks each type of work as one full-length layer. Every layer is drawn along the same fixed 240 metre length, and each layer is chosen by the file name.
sections.why: Likely reason: some schedules describe a route by type of work rather than by segment number.
sections.watch_out: Every layer has the same length, so the drawing does not show real distances along the route.

sections.name: industry_layout
sections.title: Full industry layout across zones
sections.what: Runs the recognition step, lays out each industry zone, adds unnumbered corridor work when there is no numbered linear zone, and then places the zones side by side with an 80 metre gap.
sections.why: Likely reason: keeps each industry's drawing separate while sharing one ground plan.
sections.watch_out: Corridor items are only added when there is no numbered linear zone, so adding one numbered segment switches the corridor layout off.

sections.name: _shifted
sections.title: Shifting a set of placements
sections.what: Moves every placement in a set by the same east-west and north-south amount, and rounds the new positions.
sections.why: Likely reason: lets one layout be placed next to another without rewriting its internal positions.
sections.watch_out: Shifting changes only positions, so the widths and depths in the set stay the same.

sections.name: site_layout
sections.title: Top-level site layout
sections.what: Lays out the industry zones first. Transmission lines or substations are then placed east of them, and any other leftover paths are placed south of the zones. When no industry is recognised, the paths go to the generic packing layout.
sections.why: Likely reason: the more specific layouts come first, and generic packing is the fallback.
sections.watch_out: The docstring says an empty result is returned when nothing is recognised, but the code hands the paths to the generic layout, so check which behaviour you rely on.

summary: Places schematic 3D elements for many kinds of capital project (solar, wind, process plants, mines, roads, buildings, airports, ports, dams, tunnels, water works, battery yards, telecom) by recognising element names and arranging them the way that kind of site is usually built.
purpose: Gives the viewer a plausible picture of a site when the schedule carries names but no coordinates.
why: The module docstring states that positions are display assumptions and never surveyed. The purpose is otherwise stated only in the docstring.
how: Per the docstring: a family of industry is chosen by keyword patterns, each element name is matched to a kind by an ordered list of patterns (most specific first), and each family is then placed by its own rule, such as grids, rows, flow order or a corridor. Anything unrecognised is left for the caller to pack. The placement functions are not in the sections given, so the details of their rules are not visible here.
inputs: Element names from the schedule, such as work breakdown items with numbering, and the industry family words found in them.
outputs: Placement values for each element, plus helper results for corridors, industries and whole sites. Exact types are not visible in the sections given.
risks: Keyword patterns are broad, so a word can send an element to the wrong family or kind. The list order decides ties, so a change in order changes results. Sizes are fixed guesses, so the picture is not a measurement.
debug: If an element draws as the wrong shape, find which pattern matched first in the kind list, since the earlier entry wins. If an element is missing, check its words against the family word lists. If a whole project is laid out wrongly, check the family word list for that industry. The limitation text in the output should say the layout is schematic.
